introduction-javascript-for-the-linux-ke.core: eBPF lets you run small, sandboxed programs inside the Linux kernel without writing kernel modules or rebooting, much as JavaScript lets you run code safely in a browser. Programs are loaded from user space, checked by the verifier for safety (bounded loops, valid memory access), JIT-compiled, and attached to hooks such as syscalls, kernel functions or network packets. They share data with user space through maps. This gives security tools deep, low-overhead visibility and control.

first_principles.problem: Security agents using kernel modules crash hosts and break on kernel upgrades, while user-space agents miss what happens in the kernel.

analogy.title: Browser JavaScript for the kernel
analogy.story: A browser runs untrusted scripts safely in a sandbox; eBPF runs custom logic in the kernel safely after verification.
analogy.breaks: JS can run forever; eBPF programs must be provably bounded.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Instant kernel-level visibility with no module.

code.text:
bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_execve { printf("%s -> %s\n", comm, str(args->filename)); }'
# bash -> /usr/bin/curl
# python3 -> /bin/sh   ← suspicious

check.q: What does the eBPF verifier guarantee?
check.a: That the program terminates, accesses memory safely and can't crash the kernel before it's allowed to load.

why-ebpf-the-end-of-toctou.core: Older syscall-monitoring tools (ptrace, some auditd and LD_PRELOAD approaches) inspect arguments from user space, which opens Time-Of-Check-To-Time-Of-Use (TOCTOU) races: an attacker changes the argument, such as a file path in user memory, between the security check and the kernel's actual use. eBPF can hook in-kernel functions (LSM hooks, kprobes) after arguments are copied into kernel memory, observing and enforcing on exactly what the kernel will act on, which closes that gap with low overhead.

first_principles.problem: Malware evades a ptrace-based sandbox by swapping a filename pointer in another thread after the check passes.
truths: Checks must see what's actually used.
derivation: Hook **after copy-in** (LSM, kprobes on kernel functions).
Avoid relying on **raw syscall args** in user memory.

analogy.title: Checking a cheque at the moment the bank pays out, not when it's handed over the counter
analogy.story: If you check early, someone can alter the cheque before it's cashed.
analogy.breaks: Banks check once; kernels process millions of operations per second, so hooks must be efficient.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Decisions are made on what the kernel really opens.

code.text:
sys_enter_openat(path_ptr)   ← path in user memory: raceable
security_file_open(file*)    ← LSM hook: kernel's resolved file object
# Tetragon/LSM-BPF attach here and can return -EPERM

check.q: Why is hooking security_file_open more reliable than sys_enter_openat?
check.a: It sees the kernel's resolved file object after copy-in, which user space can no longer change.

ebpf-hook-types-where-you-can-attach.core: eBPF programs attach to different hook types depending on the goal. Tracepoints are stable, predefined kernel events (sched, syscalls). Kprobes and kretprobes attach to almost any kernel function, which is powerful but unstable across versions; fentry/fexit are faster equivalents. Uprobes attach to user-space functions (such as OpenSSL's SSL_write to see plaintext). LSM hooks allow security enforcement decisions. XDP and TC hooks process network packets at line rate.

first_principles.problem: A team wants to see decrypted TLS payloads, block file writes and drop DDoS packets, and doesn't know which hooks to use.

analogy.title: Placing sensors in a building
analogy.story: Door sensors (tracepoints) are fixed, wiretaps on any cable (kprobes) are flexible but fragile, desk microphones are uprobes, guards at doors are LSM, and checkpoints at the loading dock are XDP.
analogy.breaks: Building wiring rarely changes; kernel function names change between versions.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The right hook for each goal.

code.text:
# stable syscall tracepoint
bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_connect { @[comm] = count(); }'
# kernel function
bpftrace -e 'kprobe:tcp_v4_connect { printf("%s\n", comm); }'
# user-space TLS plaintext
bpftrace -e 'uprobe:/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libssl.so.3:SSL_write { printf("%d bytes\n", arg2); }'

check.q: Which hook type would you use to read TLS plaintext?
check.a: A uprobe on the TLS library's read/write functions, such as SSL_read and SSL_write.

falco-the-security-camera.core: Falco, a CNCF project, is a runtime threat detection engine. It collects kernel events through an eBPF probe, enriches them with container and Kubernetes metadata, and evaluates them against YAML rules (shells in containers, reading /etc/shadow, unexpected outbound connections, privilege escalation). Matches produce alerts routed via Falcosidekick to Slack, SIEMs or response functions. Falco detects and alerts; it doesn't block by itself.

first_principles.problem: An attacker exploits a web app, spawns a shell and reads service-account tokens, and nobody notices.
derivation: Deploy **Falco DaemonSet** with the eBPF driver.

analogy.title: CCTV with motion detection
analogy.story: It records everything and alerts security when someone enters a restricted area, but it doesn't lock the door itself.
analogy.breaks: CCTV sees images; Falco sees syscalls enriched with container identity.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Token theft triggers a contextual critical alert.

code.text:
- rule: Read SA token by non-app process
  condition: >
    open_read and container and
    fd.name startswith /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount and
    not proc.name in (node, java)
  output: "SA token read (proc=%proc.name pod=%k8s.pod.name image=%container.image.repository)"
  priority: CRITICAL

check.q: Can Falco block a malicious process on its own?
check.a: No. It detects and alerts; blocking needs Tetragon, LSM or an automated response hook.

tetragon-the-enforcer-prevention.core: Tetragon, from Cilium/Isovalent, is eBPF-based security observability and runtime enforcement. TracingPolicies define kernel hooks (kprobes, tracepoints, LSM) with in-kernel filters on arguments, process lineage and Kubernetes identity. When a match occurs, Tetragon can act synchronously in the kernel, sending SIGKILL or overriding the return value, so the malicious action is stopped before it completes rather than alerted on afterwards. Filtering in the kernel also keeps overhead low.

first_principles.problem: By the time a detection alert fires, a crypto-miner has already started and exfiltrated keys.
truths: Async alerts are too late for some actions.
Enforcement must be precise to avoid outages.
derivation: Filter **in-kernel** by args, binary and pod.

analogy.title: A guard who tackles the intruder, versus a camera that only records them
analogy.story: Prevention acts at the moment of the attempt, not after.
analogy.breaks: Over-eager guards stop legitimate staff; policies must be tested to avoid killing real workloads.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Any write attempt to /etc kills the process in the kernel.

code.text:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1
kind: TracingPolicy
metadata: { name: protect-etc }
spec:
  kprobes:
    - call: security_file_permission
      syscall: false
      args: [{ index: 0, type: file }, { index: 1, type: int }]
      selectors:
        - matchArgs:
            - { index: 0, operator: Prefix, values: ["/etc/"] }
            - { index: 1, operator: Equal, values: ["2"] }   # MAY_WRITE
          matchActions: [{ action: Sigkill }]

check.q: Why is in-kernel Sigkill better than killing from user space after an alert?
check.a: It acts synchronously before the operation completes, avoiding the race where damage occurs first.

ebpf-security-in-kubernetes-the-full-pic.core: In Kubernetes, eBPF security spans layers. Cilium enforces identity-aware network policy (L3–L7) and transparent encryption. Tetragon observes and enforces process and file behaviour, and Falco detects threats across syscalls and the K8s audit log. All of them enrich kernel events with pod, namespace and label identity, because IPs and PIDs are ephemeral. Combined with admission policy (Gatekeeper) and image scanning, they cover the full lifecycle: build, deploy and run.

first_principles.problem: A cluster has image scanning and admission policy but no visibility into what pods actually do or connect to at runtime.
truths: Pods are ephemeral; identity must be labels, not IPs.
Network and process layers both matter.

analogy.title: A smart building's integrated security
analogy.story: Door access control, corridor cameras and room motion sensors all know which employee badge triggered them.
analogy.breaks: Buildings have fixed rooms; pods appear and vanish every few minutes.

example.title: Layered runtime defence
flow: Cilium: egress to miner pool denied

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each layer blocks or reveals part of the attack.

check.q: Why do eBPF tools enrich events with Kubernetes metadata?
check.a: IPs and PIDs are short-lived; pod, namespace and label identity make events meaningful and policies stable.
